info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 6.2: Rule-Based Normalization: Building a Deterministic Script.

questiontext.text: Why does writing an executable script audit an editor's prose orthographic policy?

generalfeedback.text: Implementing the policy audits it — every place you cannot write a rule is imprecision, genuine context-dependence, or inconsistency.

answer.text: A program requires every condition to be explicit, exposing unstated assumptions, policy imprecision, and human inconsistency.

feedback.text: Correct. Human editors easily tolerate vague rules by applying unconscious judgement; code forces every rule and boundary to be fully articulated.

answer.text: A program automatically rewrites prose policy into legal copyright terms for publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Formalizing a policy is about computational logic, not legal copyrighting.

answer.text: Running a script deletes any policy that was not written in classical Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python scripts process arbitrary text according to programmatic rules, without language restrictions.

answer.text: Code execution proves that historical scribes wrote using algorithmic grammars.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Formalization audits the modern editor's policy, not the ancient scribe's psychology.

name.text: 02 Question: The Tradition: VARD, Norma, and Transducers

questiontext.text: What critical methodological property is shared by rule-based systems like VARD 2, Norma, and finite-state transducers?

generalfeedback.text: For any rule-based output you can state which rule produced it — an inspectability that Friday's methods do not have.

answer.text: Inspectability: for every proposed normalization, the exact character rule or transformation that produced it is known and auditable.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic rule-based systems provide complete mathematical transparency, allowing readers to trace every output to a specific rule.

answer.text: They require millions of aligned training sentences before they can process a single word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule-based systems operate without neural training and work effectively on tiny datasets.

answer.text: They automatically resolve high-level syntactic and theological ambiguities without human input.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character-level transducers process tokens in isolation and cannot resolve syntactic context.

answer.text: They permanently overwrite the underlying manuscript image files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization tools operate on text and XML streams without altering image facsimiles.

name.text: 03 Question: Rule Cores and Derived Rules

questiontext.text: Why should an editor derive transformation rule cores directly from aligned <orig> and <reg> pairs?

generalfeedback.text: Derive rules from your own manual pairs — a discrepancy with your stated policy means you were applying something unstated.

answer.text: Comparing aligned pairs surfaces the actual character substitutions applied, exposing discrepancies with the editor's stated policy.

feedback.text: Correct. Deriving rules from empirical pairs reveals unstated criteria and unconscious habits that the prose policy failed to document.

answer.text: Deriving rules from pairs is required to bypass schema validation gates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML schema validation checks syntax, not how Python transformation rules were created.

answer.text: Derived rules eliminate the need to maintain a standard dictionary or lexicon.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A lexicon is still necessary to ensure that derived transformation outputs are valid words.

answer.text: Aligned pairs can only be generated by commercial cloud machine learning APIs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Aligned pairs are extracted directly from the local TEI XML file using standard Python libraries.

questiontext.text: What is the distinct role of the standard-form set within the lexicon component?

generalfeedback.text: The standard-form set is what lets a rule check its own output — without it, rules generate candidates they cannot filter.

answer.text: It allows rewrite rules to verify that their proposed output is a legitimate standard lemma rather than a fabricated non-word.

feedback.text: Correct. The standard set filters candidates generated by rewrite rules, preventing destructive nonsense transformations.

answer.text: It stores encrypted passwords for accessing remote Git repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lexicon data structure is purely linguistic and has no authentication function.

answer.text: It automatically translates Greek words into modern English glosses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization regularizes historical Greek orthography to standard Greek lemmas, not English translations.

answer.text: It replaces all polytonic Unicode characters with ASCII transliterations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The standard set contains valid polytonic Greek words in standard Unicode normalization.

questiontext.text: Why must every rewrite rule in the rule layer have an explicit condition and a unique name?

generalfeedback.text: Name every rule and require an explicit condition — the name makes output auditable and the condition stops the rule being destructive.

answer.text: The condition prevents destructive over-application to valid words, while the unique name ensures every proposed change is auditable.

feedback.text: Correct. Conditions ensure rules only fire when the input is non-standard and the output is standard; names provide full provenance in reports.

answer.text: Rule names are required by the Python compiler to allocate memory addresses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Variable names allocate memory; rule metadata strings exist for scholarly provenance.

answer.text: Explicit conditions allow the script to modify operating system file permissions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conditions evaluate string properties, not OS permissions.

answer.text: Named rules prevent the TEI document from being collated in future weeks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Auditable rule names enhance rather than hinder downstream collation.

questiontext.text: Why is generating all candidates from all rules preferable to taking the first rule match?

generalfeedback.text: Generate all candidates rather than taking the first match — ambiguity then surfaces as multiple candidates instead of being hidden by rule order.

answer.text: It avoids hidden rule-order bias and surfaces genuine ambiguity as multiple candidates rather than making an arbitrary choice.

feedback.text: Correct. Collecting all candidates ensures the script remains order-independent and transparently flags ambiguous cases for human review.

answer.text: Taking the first match crashes the Python interpreter when processing polytonic Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. First-match logic runs without crashing, but it conceals linguistic ambiguity under arbitrary execution order.

answer.text: Generating all candidates guarantees that the script achieves 100% precision on every run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generating candidates surfaces ambiguity; precision still depends on filtering and review.

answer.text: Applying all rules automatically emends scribal blunders into <corr> tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule engines regularize spelling; they do not emend mechanical blunders.

name.text: 07 Question: Weighted Edit Distance for Unseen Forms

questiontext.text: Why does the distance fallback use context-sensitive weighted Levenshtein distance rather than unweighted distance?

generalfeedback.text: Weight substitution costs by phonological plausibility — the weights are an editorial claim about the period's phonology and should be documented.

answer.text: It assigns lower costs to phonologically plausible historical substitutions (like iotacist vowel mergers), reflecting historical phonology.

feedback.text: Correct. Unweighted Levenshtein treats all letter substitutions identically; weighting encodes historical phonetic plausibility.

answer.text: Weighted distance runs ten times faster than standard Levenshtein distance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Weighted distance typically requires additional matrix lookups and is slightly slower, but far more philologically accurate.

answer.text: Unweighted distance is prohibited by the TEI Consortium guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI guidelines govern markup syntax, not mathematical distance algorithms.

answer.text: Weighted distance eliminates the need to specify a maximum distance threshold.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A threshold is still required to prevent distant, unrelated words from being proposed.

questiontext.text: Why should the normalization pipeline decline ambiguous tokens rather than guessing the most frequent candidate?

generalfeedback.text: Every decision must carry its method and reason — and where rules conflict, the script should decline rather than guess.

answer.text: A character-level script cannot evaluate syntactic context, and guessing would convert visible ambiguity into invisible errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Declining to guess routes genuinely ambiguous cases to human review, preserving the integrity of the edition.

answer.text: Declining ambiguous tokens prevents the script from saving output to disk.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Declined tokens are recorded cleanly in structured JSON reports.

answer.text: Python functions are structurally unable to make probabilistic selections between two strings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python can easily select randomly or by frequency, but doing so without context introduces silent errors.

answer.text: Moodle XML question banks reject any quiz that contains ambiguous Greek words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Question banks handle arbitrary text; declining is an editorial standard for the TEI edition.

name.text: 09 Question: Running It Over Your Text

questiontext.text: Why should the script emit structured JSON proposals rather than modifying TEI XML directly?

generalfeedback.text: Have the script emit structured proposals rather than modified XML — mixing machine and human decisions in one state destroys the comparison.

answer.text: It keeps machine proposals distinct from human decisions, allowing rigorous evaluation before any changes touch the edition.

feedback.text: Correct. The script proposes and the editor disposes; direct modification would blend unverified machine outputs into the scholarly text.

answer.text: JSON is the only file format accepted by TEI schema validators.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas validate XML documents, not JSON files.

answer.text: Modifying XML files directly permanently locks the operating system file system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File systems allow direct XML modification; the separation is a philological safeguard.

answer.text: Emitting JSON prevents the editor from viewing the results in a terminal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON output can be easily inspected, formatted, and summarized in any terminal.

name.text: 10 Question: Measuring Against Your Manual Work

questiontext.text: When evaluating a normalization script against a manual baseline, why is high precision with low recall preferable to high recall with low precision?

generalfeedback.text: High precision with low recall is useful; high recall with low precision is worse than useless — a single accuracy figure hides which you have.

answer.text: High-precision proposals can be trusted with minimal review, whereas low-precision output generates false positives that cost more to correct than working by hand.

feedback.text: Correct. A safe, conservative script automates clear cases without burdening the editor with auditing hundreds of destructive over-applications.

answer.text: High recall guarantees that the script will never encounter an unknown Greek word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recall measures performance on existing variants, not total lexicon coverage.

answer.text: Low precision indicates that the script ran faster and used less system memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precision measures correctness, not computational execution speed.

answer.text: Precision and recall are identical metrics that always produce the exact same percentage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precision is true positives over all proposals; recall is true positives over all target variants.

questiontext.text: Why is a script's inability to distinguish period-normal usage (<orig>) from scribal slips (<sic>) a method limitation rather than a software bug?

generalfeedback.text: Distinguish implementation failures from method limitations — a script structurally cannot tell period-normal usage from a scribal slip.

answer.text: The distinction depends on historical knowledge of contemporary acceptability rather than character-string properties.

feedback.text: Correct. A character-level script operates purely on letter patterns; determining whether a spelling was acceptable in its period requires historical context.

answer.text: The Python language does not support conditional statements for Greek text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python supports full Unicode logic; the limitation is semantic and historical.

answer.text: The distinction was invented in the 21st century and did not exist in antiquity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribal blunders vs. phonetic spellings were recognized distinctions in antiquity.

answer.text: Distinguishing errors from variants requires hardware acceleration on dedicated GPUs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The limitation is theoretical knowledge, not compute hardware.

questiontext.text: What does it indicate when the script flags ambiguity on a token that the human editor regularized without hesitation?

generalfeedback.text: Ambiguities the script finds where you hesitated not at all mark where your judgement uses context your stated rules do not capture.

answer.text: The editor used contextual syntactic understanding without realizing it, showing that the decision was less mechanical than the stated policy implied.

feedback.text: Correct. The editor unconsciously drew on sentence context, revealing the boundary where character rules fail and contextual analysis begins.

answer.text: The human editor committed an egregious blunder that must be penalized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The human editor applied valid philological judgement; the comparison merely highlights tacit context.

answer.text: The Python regex engine encountered an unhandled encoding exception.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The script performed correctly by identifying multiple valid rule candidates.

answer.text: The manuscript passage must be discarded from the critical edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ambiguous tokens are standard editorial phenomena that simply require documentation.

questiontext.text: Why do rule-based systems like Norma achieve high accuracy on small datasets (~100 tokens) where neural models struggle?

generalfeedback.text: Rule-based systems reach 83% accuracy from 100 tokens — at your scale today's method may simply be the better tool, not the primitive one.

answer.text: Hand-crafted and derived rules generalize patterns from very few examples without requiring large corpora of training data.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic rules capture phonetic principles directly, whereas neural sequence models starve without thousands of aligned pairs.

answer.text: Rule-based systems download pre-trained weights from cloud neural networks during execution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule-based systems rely on explicit logic and lexicons, not neural weights.

answer.text: Historical manuscripts never contain more than 100 total words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscripts typically contain thousands of words, but individual student projects work on small sample folios.

answer.text: Neural models refuse to execute on any computer running Linux.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neural models run natively on Linux; the limitation is dataset size.

questiontext.text: Why must an editor avoid tuning a script until it achieves 100% agreement with their manual decisions on a single folio?

generalfeedback.text: Do not tune until the script reproduces your decisions exactly — where it disagrees, check whether your decision followed your own policy.

answer.text: Over-tuning fits the script to the idiosyncrasies of one folio rather than implementing a general, transferable orthographic policy.

feedback.text: Correct. Over-fitting encodes accidental human choices; where script and human disagree, the editor must verify whether the human followed the policy.

answer.text: Achieving 100% agreement causes Git to corrupt the commit history DAG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git records repository states regardless of script accuracy percentages.

answer.text: A script with 100% accuracy is automatically flagged as plagiarism by university servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Over-fitting is a methodological error in generalization, not academic dishonesty.

answer.text: The TEI schema rejects any XML file that was generated by a script with perfect recall.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate XML grammar, not script evaluation metrics.

name.text: 15 Question: When the Script Is Right and You Were Not

questiontext.text: How does running a uniform deterministic script improve the quality of a manual edition?

generalfeedback.text: The script's uniformity catches your inconsistency — the deterministic step improves the manual one, not only the reverse.

answer.text: The script's uniform application surfaces instances where human fatigue or distraction caused identical variants to be missed or treated inconsistently.

feedback.text: Correct. Human editors tire and miss words; the script applies rules relentlessly across the whole text, catching human oversights.

answer.text: The script rewrites the text to match modern English grammar automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The script regularizes historical orthography according to the editor's Greek rules.

answer.text: The script eliminates the need for human editors to verify transcriptions against manuscript facsimiles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All script proposals still require human verification against the primary witness.

answer.text: The script changes all Greek font glyphs to match twentieth-century print typography.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization deals with text strings and Unicode code points, not font rendering.

name.text: 16 Question: Projecting the Results into TEI

questiontext.text: How should accepted machine regularizations be attributed in TEI XML to ensure scholarly reproducibility?

generalfeedback.text: Attribute machine regularizations to a named script at a named commit — 'generated by a script' is not reproducible attribution.

answer.text: Use @resp="#script" and declare #script in the header with the exact script name, rule version, and Git commit hash.

feedback.text: Correct. Naming the exact script and commit hash allows future researchers to reproduce and verify the exact automated procedure.

answer.text: Attribute all changes to @resp="#anonymous" to protect the author's privacy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly provenance requires explicit identification of editorial agents.

answer.text: Embed the entire Python script inside an XML comment on every line of the transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Script details belong in the header <respStmt>, not duplicated in line comments.

answer.text: Delete the <orig> element whenever a machine regularization is accepted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both <orig> and <reg> must be preserved in <choice>.

name.text: 17 Question: Logging the Method in the Header

questiontext.text: Why should the script's measured precision and recall be documented in the TEI header's <editorialDecl>?

generalfeedback.text: Record the script's measured precision and recall in the header — a reader cannot otherwise judge how much weight the <reg> layer bears.

answer.text: It informs readers of the empirical reliability of the regularized layer, allowing them to judge how much confidence it warrants.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparency about automated performance provides crucial context for downstream scholars using the regularized text.

answer.text: It is required by web browsers to render polytonic Greek fonts correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browser rendering depends on font support and CSS, not header editorial declarations.

answer.text: It allows the TEI file to be automatically converted into a binary executable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI files are scholarly XML documents, not compiled binaries.

answer.text: Documenting metrics allows the editor to skip writing the assignment report.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Header documentation is part of the edition; the assignment requires detailed analysis.

name.text: 18 Question: What the Script Cannot Do

questiontext.text: Why is measuring recall on the same folio from which rules were derived an optimistic estimate?

generalfeedback.text: Recall measured on the folio the rules came from is optimistic — test on a folio you did not use, and report the drop.

answer.text: The rules were tailored to variation observed on that training folio; unseen folios or scribal hands may present unanticipated patterns.

feedback.text: Correct. Testing on training data measures memorization; testing on unseen folios reveals true generalization capability.

answer.text: Folios in the same manuscript are written in completely different alphabets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The alphabet remains Greek; specific orthographic habits and scribal hands vary.

answer.text: The Python regex engine degrades in accuracy after processing 300 words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software performance does not degrade over text length.

answer.text: Unseen folios are legally protected by copyright and cannot be evaluated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical manuscripts are in the public domain; generalization testing is standard.

questiontext.text: Why is it valuable to create normalization/comparison.json covering tokens across manual and script passes before Friday?

generalfeedback.text: Build the per-token comparison table today so Friday's AI proposals become a column rather than a new analysis.

answer.text: It establishes a structured per-token matrix so Friday's AI proposals can be added as a column for direct three-way evaluation.

feedback.text: Correct. Having manual and script decisions pre-aligned allows immediate, systematic comparison when model outputs are generated.

answer.text: It prevents language models from generating unauthorized API billing charges.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON tables organize evaluation data; API billing is managed through provider accounts.

answer.text: It converts polytonic Greek into modern monotonic Greek automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The comparison matrix preserves exact historical and regularized spellings.

answer.text: It replaces the need to commit project files to Git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version control discipline is essential throughout the entire workflow.

questiontext.text: Why must the normalization script be executed against the diplomatic consensus text rather than yesterday's manually normalized file?

generalfeedback.text: Run the script against the diplomatic base rather than the normalized text, or you measure it against its own target.

answer.text: Running against already normalized text would evaluate the script on its own target, producing meaningless accuracy figures.

feedback.text: Correct. The script must process the unregularized diplomatic base to test whether it independently identifies and resolves variants.

answer.text: The script will crash if it encounters a valid XML tag in the input file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The script parses XML or extracts text tokens without crashing.

answer.text: Yesterday's normalized file was automatically deleted during Git tagging.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git preserves all committed files and tagged states permanently.

answer.text: Running against diplomatic text is prohibited by university academic integrity guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluating automated tools on raw inputs is standard scientific method.

questiontext.text: What is the most likely cause if a normalization script executes cleanly but proposes zero regularizations across the entire text?

generalfeedback.text: A script proposing nothing looks identical to a text needing nothing — test with a known non-standard token before trusting a clean run.

answer.text: A Unicode normalization mismatch (e.g., text in NFC and lexicon in NFD), causing string equality checks to fail silently.

feedback.text: Correct. Visually identical characters in different Unicode normal forms do not match in Python; applying NFC normalization at all boundaries fixes this.

answer.text: The computer processor ran out of floating-point registers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. String matching uses basic memory and integer operations, not floating-point limits.

answer.text: The manuscript contains too many lines of text for Python to process.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python easily processes millions of lines; a single folio is tiny.

answer.text: The Git repository was initialized with an incorrect user email address.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git metadata does not affect script regex execution.

name.text: 22 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a genuine scientific evaluation of a normalization script from a superficial demonstration?

generalfeedback.text: Using the comparison to correct your own inconsistencies is what makes it an evaluation rather than a demonstration.

answer.text: Categorizing failures, separating implementation bugs from structural method limits, and using discrepancies to correct manual inconsistencies.

feedback.text: Correct. Rigorous evaluation investigates why disagreements occurred and uses the comparison to refine both the code and the edition.

answer.text: Claiming 100% precision and recall without reporting any ambiguous cases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Concealing ambiguity and claiming flawless performance indicates uncritical over-fitting.

answer.text: Writing the script in assembly language rather than Python.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Choice of programming language does not determine scholarly rigor.

answer.text: Deleting the decision log once the script runs without syntax errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Preserving the decision log is vital for transparency and auditability.

questiontext.text: Why does a rule-based regularized layer constitute stronger scholarly evidence than an unconstrained neural model output?

generalfeedback.text: A rule-based <reg> is a claim the reader can check; a neural one is a claim they must trust — which matters independently of accuracy.

answer.text: A rule-based output can be independently inspected, verified, and contested against explicit rules, whereas an opaque neural output must be taken on trust.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly editions are arguments; an argument whose steps can be inspected and audited is inherently stronger than a black-box assertion.

answer.text: Rule-based outputs are protected by international diplomatic immunity treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly strength derives from transparency and reproducibility, not legal treaties.

answer.text: Neural models can only output modern English text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neural models output Greek, but their internal decision steps cannot be audited.

answer.text: Rule-based scripts are immune to human typing errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human editors write rules, but explicit rules allow mistakes to be detected and corrected.

questiontext.text: According to contemporary computational philology, what is the optimal division of labor in historical text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: The literature's position is hybrid — rules for deterministic substitution, models for context, humans for the variant-versus-error judgement.

answer.text: Rule-based transducers for deterministic phonetic transformations, language models for syntactic disambiguation, and humans for the variant-versus-error decision.

feedback.text: Correct. The hybrid architecture leverages the unique strengths of each method: rules for verifiable substitutions, AI for context, humans for philological judgement.

answer.text: Generative AI models handle 100% of the text while human editors only handle marketing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unconstrained AI models over-normalize and erase linguistic data; human oversight is essential.

answer.text: Rule-based scripts are used exclusively for deleting damaged manuscript folios.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule scripts perform linguistic regularization, not document destruction.

answer.text: All normalization is banned in favor of unreadable diplomatic ASCII transcripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern scholarship values both diplomatic fidelity and regularized searchability via TEI.

questiontext.text: How does the deterministic rule baseline function as a detector for generative over-normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Your rule baseline is the detector for Friday's over-normalization — a large deviation from character-level substitution marks where the model altered meaning.

answer.text: It flags large deviations from character-level reachability, alerting the editor when a model alters morphology or substitutes modern synonyms.

feedback.text: Correct. Because rules only perform character-level substitutions, proposals unreachable by rules mark where a model crossed into semantic alteration.

answer.text: It automatically blocks the computer from connecting to the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The baseline is a comparative evaluation tool, not a network firewall.

answer.text: It sends an alert to the TEI Consortium whenever an AI model is queried.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluation occurs locally within the project repository.

answer.text: It deletes any JSON file that contains Greek characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON files are used to store and evaluate model proposals.

name.text: 26 Question: Synthesis: Rules as Explicit Editorial Practice

questiontext.text: What is the ultimate intellectual value of encoding normalization rules as a deterministic program?

generalfeedback.text: Writing the rules made your tacit editorial practice explicit — what survived is policy, and what did not is either genuine context-dependence or inconsistency you did not know about.

answer.text: It transforms tacit human editorial intuitions into explicit, reproducible scholarly claims that can be audited and refined.

feedback.text: Correct. Formalization forces clarity, separating consistent policy from subjective inconsistency and isolating genuine syntactic ambiguity.

answer.text: It guarantees that digital humanities students will never need to read Greek manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital methods deepen philological engagement rather than replacing manuscript reading.

answer.text: It proves that computer programs understand the theological meaning of ancient texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule scripts execute string transformations without semantic comprehension.

answer.text: It allows critical editions to be published without editorial documentation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documentation is essential to explain and defend the chosen rule set.

questiontext.text: Why does a committed rule script provide a long-term reproducibility guarantee that hosted commercial AI models cannot offer?

generalfeedback.text: Your script's output can be re-derived indefinitely; a hosted model's cannot — which means claims resting on it may become underivable.

answer.text: The committed script and lexicon can be re-executed identically for decades, whereas commercial API models drift, change, or become unavailable.

feedback.text: Correct. A scholarly edition resting on hosted model calls risks having its evidentiary foundation evaporate when the proprietary API changes.

answer.text: Commercial AI models are deleted every evening at midnight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hosted models persist across versions, but proprietary updates cause behavioral drift and eventual deprecation.

answer.text: Python scripts are legally required to remain identical under international law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reproducibility is a technical property of local code and data, not a legal statute.

answer.text: Rule scripts cannot run on computers manufactured after 2026.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard Python code possesses exceptionally long backward compatibility.

questiontext.text: When scaling a rule-based normalization script to subsequent manuscript folios, why must the rule set version be recorded per batch?

generalfeedback.text: Record which rule set version normalized each folio — otherwise the edition is inconsistent in a way nobody can detect.

answer.text: Rule sets evolve over time; without version tracking, different folios are regularized under different policies without any audit trail.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording rule versions (e.g., v3 vs. v7) in commit logs ensures that policy evolution remains transparent across the entire edition.

answer.text: The TEI schema requires every XML file to be compiled with a different Python version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML validation is independent of the Python interpreter version used.

answer.text: Recording version numbers increases the computational clock speed of the script.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version tracking is metadata discipline, not a hardware optimization.

answer.text: Git refuses to commit any file that does not contain a software release tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks changes regardless of version tags; recording versions is an editorial standard.

name.text: 29 Question: What This Week Is Actually Testing

questiontext.text: Why does evaluating a normalization method differ fundamentally from evaluating a transcription method?

generalfeedback.text: Normalization has no fact of the matter, so the stated policy is the standard — which is why documentation matters more here than in transcription.

answer.text: Transcription has a physical fact of the matter (the ink), whereas normalization measures consistency against a chosen, stated editorial policy.

feedback.text: Correct. Accuracy in normalization is relative to the editor's stated policy rather than an objective external document.

answer.text: Transcription is subjective poetry, whereas normalization is objective mathematics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcription is objective reading of physical ink; normalization involves subjective policy choices.

answer.text: Normalization requires learning Latin, whereas transcription only applies to Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both operations apply equally to Greek, Latin, and other historical languages.

answer.text: Transcription files cannot be stored in Git repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All project stages are tracked in Git.

questiontext.text: What is the overarching conclusion of Lesson 6.2 regarding rule-based normalization?

generalfeedback.text: The script's value is a verifiable baseline and an audit of your own consistency — not merely automation of what you already did.

answer.text: Rule-based scripts provide an inspectable, reproducible, and verifiable baseline that audits human consistency and serves as a detector for AI errors.

feedback.text: Correct. The deterministic script is not a crude precursor to AI, but a necessary, transparent baseline that makes rigorous evaluation possible.

answer.text: Rule-based scripts should replace all human editors and language models in textual scholarship.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rules cannot handle syntactic ambiguity or determine historical acceptability; a hybrid workflow is necessary.

answer.text: Rule-based normalization is obsolete and should never be used in digital humanities projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rules remain the gold standard for transparency, low-resource performance, and auditability.

answer.text: Scripts should only be used if they achieve 100% precision and recall on the first attempt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Discrepancies and limitations are expected and provide valuable analytical insights.
